about: Player-facing fact cards for Diamond Springs. Each restates one audited, confirmed question from games/trivia/data/questions.json (id). tools/check-facts.mjs verifies ids, confidence and sources. hs-0231 is shown only as a history card in the Fact Album, never in play.

facts.text: In 1886 the Chicago White Stockings came to Hot Springs for spring training, the first major league club to train there.
The Chicago White Stockings who trained in Hot Springs in 1886 are known today as the Chicago Cubs.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: Baseball's Golden Days in Hot Springs

facts.text: White Stockings president Albert Spalding decided to train his team in a warmer climate. Cap Anson was the playing-manager.
facts.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Major League Spring Training in Hot Springs

facts.text: Future evangelist Billy Sunday was a member of the 1886 White Stockings trip to Hot Springs.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: Hot Springs Baseball Grounds

facts.text: Hot Springs has been called the birthplace of spring training, but it was not unquestionably the first: the New York Mutuals went to New Orleans, perhaps the first team to train away from home.
Cap Anson hit three home runs at the Hot Springs Baseball Grounds on March 28, 1887.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: Hot Springs Baseball Grounds

facts.text: Hot Springs' Whittington Park ballfield opened in 1894, replacing the Hot Springs Baseball Grounds.
Whittington Park's right-field fence was 260 feet from home plate. Left field was 340 feet and center 400 feet.
Lights were installed at Whittington Park in 1936. The right-field fence was raised 15 feet in 1938.
From 1921 to 1923 Whittington Park was called McKee Park. It took back the Whittington name from 1924 to 1935.
In 1935 Whittington Park was renamed for American League founder Ban Johnson.
The Pittsburgh Pirates trained at Whittington Park from 1901 to 1916.
In 1912 baseball star Honus Wagner bought and donated basketball uniforms to Hot Springs High School, in the Pirates' black and gold.
In 1909 Red Sox owner John I. Taylor built the stands at Hot Springs' Majestic Park and signed a five-year lease on the site.
The Detroit Tigers first created a practice field on the Majestic Park site in 1908. The original park was demolished in 1918.
During their years training at Majestic Park, the Red Sox won the World Series in 1912, 1915, 1916 and 1918.
Fogel Field was built in 1912 to meet the demand of over 250 major leaguers training in Hot Springs.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: Fogel Field, built in 1912 by the Hot Springs Park Company, is also known as Fordyce Field.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: On March 17, 1918, Babe Ruth hit a home run at Whittington Park that landed in the Arkansas Alligator Farm.
In 2011 B&F Engineering measured Ruth's 1918 home run at about 573 feet. A Boston newspaper at the time thought it went more than 500 feet.
facts.source: KNWA/KFTA: The home run that made Babe Ruth a star

facts.text: Baseball historian Bill Jenkinson helped authenticate the estimated 573-foot figure, but said no one can confirm it with complete certainty.
Though mainly a pitcher, Babe Ruth played first base in that March 17, 1918, exhibition.
facts.source: KNWA/KFTA: The home run that made Babe Ruth a star

facts.text: Ruth's famous 1918 home run came in the sixth inning. It flew over the right-field fence and across the street.
facts.source: KNWA/KFTA: The home run that made Babe Ruth a star

facts.text: Ruth's first home run of March 17, 1918, landed in a wood pile. His second landed in the Alligator Farm.
The Red Sox played Brooklyn in Babe Ruth's March 17, 1918, exhibition at Whittington Park.
facts.source: KNWA/KFTA: The home run that made Babe Ruth a star

facts.text: The Arkansas Alligator Farm was founded on Whittington Avenue in 1902.
Per the Historic Baseball Trail, Babe Ruth trained in Hot Springs nine times.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: The Hot Springs Arlingtons, a Black baseball club, played at Whittington Park from 1896 to 1903. The Hot Springs Blues followed in 1904.
The Pittsburgh Crawfords trained at Hot Springs' Fogel Field from 1932 to 1935. The Homestead Grays had trained there in 1930–31.
Sam Guinn Field opened in 1933 at 497 Crescent Avenue to host Negro league spring training.
The Sam Guinn Field trail marker names Negro league clubs that trained there, including the Kansas City Monarchs, the Pittsburgh Crawfords and the Homestead Grays.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: Hank Aaron, 18, played a 1952 Negro League World Series game in Hot Springs with the Indianapolis Clowns.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: The Ray Doan (All-Star) Baseball School ran in Hot Springs from 1933 to 1938. Attendance peaked at 450 in 1938.
Babe Didrikson attended Hot Springs' Ray Doan baseball school in 1934. Instructors included Rogers Hornsby and Bob Feller.
Hot Springs' George Barr school (1935–47) is recognized as the first school for umpires.
Rogers Hornsby ran a "Baseball College" in Hot Springs from 1939, based at Majestic Field.
The Hot Springs Bathers played in the Class C Cotton States League in 1938–41 and 1947–55.
The Hot Springs Bathers won Cotton States League titles in 1941, 1948 and 1950.
Hot Springs' professional baseball team in 1906 was the Hot Springs Vapors. The Vaporites followed in 1908–09.
More than 130 Hall of Famers played or trained at Whittington/Ban Johnson Park, including Cy Young, Ty Cobb, Walter Johnson and Satchel Paige.
Arkansas-born Hall of Fame catcher Bill Dickey was discovered subbing in a semi-pro game at Whittington Park.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: On March 18, 1912, Tris Speaker homered over Whittington Park's left-field fence.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: Tris Speaker

facts.text: Sam "Wahoo" Crawford, the MLB career triples leader, played a 1911 exhibition at Whittington Park.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: Slugger Al Simmons credited Hot Springs' baths and trails with saving his career.
facts.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

facts.text: A Weyerhaeuser parking lot now covers the site of old Ban Johnson Park. A home-plate marker remains.
Cement bleachers called the "Wolves Den" survive on the hillside at the old Ban Johnson Park site.
The rebuilt Majestic Park was completed in spring 2021, after voters passed a bond issue in September 2019.
The modern Majestic Park in Hot Springs has five baseball fields, plus grandstands, batting cages and playgrounds.
Hot Springs sought an $8.5 million bond for the renovation of Majestic Park. A $500,000 grant from the Oaklawn Foundation helped start it.
National Park College uses Majestic Park as its home baseball field.
The First Boys of Spring, a 2015 documentary about Hot Springs baseball, was narrated by Billy Bob Thornton.

In 1953 Cotton States League owners tried to expel the Hot Springs Bathers for signing brothers Jim and Leander Tugerson. The eviction was not permanent, but the brothers never played a regular-season game for Hot Springs.
